screens.title: Introduction to Software Engineering & Version Control with Git
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson we move beyond writing isolated programs and learn how software engineering and version control help teams build reliable systems. Software engineering brings structure: it uses modularity to break a large problem into smaller parts, abstraction to hide unneeded details, and reusability to avoid rewriting common code. These practices make projects easier to test, maintain, and scale. Version control, and specifically Git, complements engineering by tracking every change, enabling safe experiments, and allowing teams to merge contributions without losing work. You will see how the working directory, staging area, and local repository form a simple pipeline for tracking snapshots with commands like init, add, commit, status, and log. You will also practice cloning a remote repo and sharing work with push and pull. By the end of this chapter you will be able to initialize a repository, stage and commit changes thoughtfully, read the commit history, and follow a basic collaborative workflow. This foundation is essential because confident use of Git prevents lost work and makes team development predictable. Ready to explore these practical skills and try a first Git project?

Second, you'll understand why version control systems are essential in projects, including how they prevent lost work, provide a history of changes, and enable collaboration. You will learn to stage changes deliberately using git add so you choose which edits enter the next snapshot. You will write clear commit messages that explain intent and help later debugging. screens.title: What is Software Engineering?
screens.narratorSegment: Software engineering is a systematic, disciplined, and quantifiable approach to creating software that works reliably over time and across teams. At its core are principles you already know in code form: modularity breaks a large system into smaller, testable components so one change does not destabilize everything; abstraction hides implementation details so modules communicate through clear interfaces; and reusability lets you use the same component in multiple places instead of copying logic. A concrete example is designing a logging module for a Java application. Instead of sprinkling print statements throughout the code, a logging module offers a simple interface: log message and log level. Different parts of the app depend on that interface, so changing how logs are written does not require editing every class. A common misconception is that software engineering is only for large teams; in fact, these practices benefit solo projects by making them easier to navigate and extend. In practice, software engineering reduces bugs, improves onboarding for new developers, and shortens time to add new features. Reflect: when you next create a class, ask whether that class belongs to a reusable module, and how you would test it independently.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › What is Software Engineering?
Core Definition
A disciplined approach that makes software predictable, testable, and maintainable.
Modularity
Split systems into small components that can be developed and tested independently.
Abstraction
Expose minimal interfaces and hide internal complexity to reduce coupling.
Reusability
Design components so they can be used across the codebase instead of copied.
Concrete Example — Logging Module
// Logger.java (conceptual)
public interface Logger {
  void info(String message);
  void error(String message);
}

// Implementation can change without touching callers
Benefit
Easier testing and safer changes.
Misconception
Engineering is only for big teams; small projects gain clarity too.
Key Takeaway

Apply modularity and abstraction early: they pay off as code grows and teams form.

screens.title: What is a Version Control System?
screens.narratorSegment: A Version Control System records changes to files over time so you can recall specific versions later. It serves three practical needs: history, collaboration, and safety. History helps you understand how and why the code evolved; collaboration lets multiple people work on the same codebase without overwriting one another; safety provides undo and branching so experiments don't break the mainline. Git is a distributed VCS, which means every developer has a full copy of the repository and its history on their machine. This local history enables fast operations and offline work. An everyday example is fixing a bug introduced two weeks ago: you use the commit history to find the change, inspect the commit message and diff, and then either revert or fix the faulty commit. A common misconception is to rely solely on file copies or zip backups; these lack structured history, metadata, and a reliable way to merge parallel work. With Git, you can branch to try a new feature, merge it once it's stable, and keep the main branch clean. Think about the last time you lost work; a VCS avoids that scenario by making snapshots explicit and reversible.

keyIdea.title: VCS Role
keyIdea.text: A VCS like Git stores change history, supports branches for parallel work, and enables collaboration with remotes.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › What is a VCS?
Version Control System — Practical View
It records snapshots and metadata, enabling recall, branching, and collaboration.
History
Track who changed what and when, so bugs are easier to trace.
Collaboration
Multiple contributors can work concurrently with a merging strategy.
Safety
Experiment with branches and revert changes if an experiment fails.
Distributed VCS note: With Git, every developer has a full repository copy locally, which makes many operations fast and resilient to network issues.
Analogy
Think of a VCS like a ledger that records transactions for a project. Each commit is a ledger entry describing a change.
Common Mistake
Using file copies or manual backups instead of a VCS loses metadata like who changed the file and why, and makes merges error-prone.
Key Takeaway

Use a VCS to make history explicit, support branching, and enable reliable team workflows.

screens.title: Git Local Workflow: Working Directory → Staging → Local Repository
screens.narratorSegment: Git tracks file changes through three clear states: modified, staged, and committed. The working directory is where you edit files; changes there are local edits and not yet part of any snapshot. When you decide which edits go into the next snapshot, you stage them with git add. The staging area acts as a curated buffer so you can assemble a specific set of changes for a single logical commit. Finally, git commit writes those staged changes into the local repository as an immutable snapshot with a message describing intent. A concrete example: you add a feature and fix a typo in two separate files. By staging only the feature file, you can commit it with a focused message and stage the typo separately for its own commit. This keeps history meaningful. A common misconception is to assume git commit auto-includes all modified files; without git add, modifications remain unstaged and will not be captured. Practice the habit: edit, git status to inspect, git add the intended files, then git commit with a descriptive message. This three-step discipline leads to clear history, easier code review, and safer collaboration.

keyIdea.title: Workflow
keyIdea.text: Use the three Git states to curate commits: edit in the working directory, stage deliberately, then commit snapshots to the local repository.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Local Workflow
Three States Explained
Modified: Your working directory contains edits that Git knows about but has not yet staged.
Staged: You used git add to mark selected changes for inclusion in the next commit.
Committed: git commit wrote the staged changes into the local repository as a snapshot with metadata.
Quick Command Checklist
git status   # inspect modified and staged files
git add   # stage specific file
git commit -m "Descriptive message"  # create a snapshot
Practical Example
You change HelloWorld.java to add a second print line and fix README. Stage only the code change before committing to keep history focused.
# Inspect
git status

# Stage only the code change
git add HelloWorld.java

# Commit the code change
git commit -m "Add a second print statement to HelloWorld"

# Stage and commit README separately
git add README.md
git commit -m "Update project README"
Misconception: Committing without staging includes all edits. Reality: Only staged changes are committed.

screens.title: Initialize a Repository and Make Your First Commit
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through initializing a repository and making your first commits using a simple Java example. First, create a project directory in the terminal and run git init. This creates a hidden. git folder that stores the repository metadata. Next, create HelloWorld. java with a print statement. At this point git status will show HelloWorld. java as untracked. Use git add HelloWorld. java to stage it and then run git commit -m with a clear message describing the addition. After the commit, git status will show a clean working directory and git log will display the commit with its hash, author, date, and message. A concrete example in the terminal: mkdir MyJavaProject, cd into it, git init, create the Java file, git status, git add, git commit -m "Initial commit: Added HelloWorld. java". A common beginner mistake is committing without adding files, which either creates an empty commit or misses changes. Always run git status before committing to confirm which files are staged. End by asking: can you read the commit message you just wrote and understand the change it documents?

keyIdea.title: Practice Command
keyIdea.text: Initialize with git init, stage with git add, and snapshot with git commit to build a clear local history.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Init & First Commit
Terminal Demo (Conceptual)
Follow these commands to create a tracked project and your first commit.
mkdir MyJavaProject
cd MyJavaProject
git init

# Create HelloWorld.java and then:
git status
# You should see: untracked files: HelloWorld.java

git add HelloWorld.java
git commit -m "Initial commit: Added HelloWorld.java"

# Verify history
git log
Explanation
git init prepares the directory; git add stages; git commit records a snapshot with a message. The hidden .git folder stores history.
Pro Tip
Run git status before committing to confirm exactly what will be recorded.
Key Takeaway

Initialize early and commit small, meaningful units of work to keep history useful.

screens.title: Working Directory vs Staging Area vs Local Repository
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the difference between the working directory, staging area, and local repository is essential for predictable commits. The working directory contains the files you edit; they are your current working copy. The staging area, or index, is where you gather the specific changes you want to include in the next commit; think of it as a packing area for a snapshot. The local repository stores committed snapshots permanently on your machine's. git directory. When you run git status, Git lists files by these states, showing untracked, modified, and staged files. A practical example: if you change two files but only stage one, the commit will include only the staged file. This separation lets you craft commits that represent single logical changes—ideal for code review and debugging. A common mistake is to commit a large mixed-change snapshot with unrelated edits. To avoid this, use git add for the intended changes and commit frequently with clear messages. Reading git status and then using git diff for unstaged changes or git diff --staged for what's staged helps you verify the exact contents of a commit before creating it.

keyIdea.title: State Contrast
keyIdea.text: Use git status and diff tools to confirm which edits are staged and which remain only in your working directory before committing.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › States Comparison
Working Directory
Your editable files on disk. Changes appear here immediately when you save files in your editor.
Commands to inspect:
git status git diff
Staging Area (Index)
A buffer where selected changes wait to be committed. Use it to group related edits into a single commit.
Commands to inspect:
git add git diff --staged
Local Repository
The .git database of commits stored on your machine. Commits here are persistent snapshots with metadata.
Commands to inspect:
git commit -m "msg" git log
Practical Rule
Stage only related changes and commit often. Before committing, run git status and diff to ensure the snapshot contains the intended edits.

screens.title: Inspecting History: git status and git log
screens.narratorSegment: Two commands you will use constantly are git status and git log. git status reports the current state of your working directory and staging area, listing untracked, modified, and staged files. It helps you decide what to add or commit. git log shows the sequence of commits in the current branch, including each commit's hash, author, date, and message. A practical pattern is to run git status before you stage changes and to view git log after commits to confirm that the message and snapshot reflect your intent. For example, after committing an initial HelloWorld. java, git log shows your initial commit message and hash, which you can use later to reference that snapshot. A common mistake is skimming the message without confirming the diff; always use git log in combination with git show or git diff between commits to inspect the exact changes. Clear commit messages and frequent logs make it straightforward to find when a bug was introduced, who made the change, and what the rationale was. Ending question: which commit in your log best explains why a change was made?

keyIdea.text: Use git status to prepare commits and git log with diff tools to investigate past changes and their context.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Inspecting History
git status
Shows files that are untracked, modified, or staged so you can decide your next action.
# Typical output (conceptual)
On branch main
Untracked files:
  HelloWorld.java
Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged ..." to unstage)
    new file: HelloWorld.java
git log
Shows past commits. Use git show or git diff to inspect the contents of a specific commit.
commit 9fceb02
Author: You 
Date:   2024-06-01

    Initial commit: Added HelloWorld.java
Practice Tip
Combine git log with git show to review the exact changes and confirm the rationale captured by the commit message.

screens.title: Remote Repositories: clone, push, and pull
screens.narratorSegment: Remote repositories hosted on services provide a central source of truth for collaboration. To get a copy of a remote repository, use git clone with the repository URL; this creates a local copy and sets the remote origin. After making local commits, use git push to upload your commits to the remote so teammates can see and integrate your work. To receive others' changes, use git pull which fetches changes and merges them into your local branch. Remember that git pull performs a fetch followed by a merge; you can also run git fetch then inspect and merge manually when you want more control. A practical pattern is: clone, create a feature branch locally, commit small units of work, pull regularly from main to stay current, resolve conflicts if needed, and push your feature branch for review. A common mistake is forgetting to pull before pushing; this can produce rejected pushes due to divergent histories and forces a merge or rebase. Practice pulling frequently and communicate with your team about branch usage. Ask yourself: how will you avoid conflicting changes if two people edit the same file in parallel?

keyIdea.title: Remote Workflow
keyIdea.text: Clone to start, pull to receive updates, and push to share your commits. Pull frequently to minimize merge conflicts.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Remotes & Collaboration
Commands Summary
# Get a remote copy
git clone 

# After commits, share them
git push origin main

# Receive changes from remote
git pull origin main
git clone copies both files and full history. git push uploads your local commits, and git pull fetches and merges remote updates. Use feature branches and pull requests on the remote platform to coordinate reviews and merges.
Common Mistake
Pushing without pulling first can cause rejected pushes or complicated merges. Pull regularly to avoid divergence.
Practice Scenario
Two devs edit the same file. If you pull frequently you will likely detect and resolve conflicts with small changes, keeping merges manageable.
Key Takeaway

Remotes enable teamwork. Use clone, push, and pull with clear branch strategies to collaborate effectively.

screens.title: Hands-on: Your First Git Project Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: We'll simulate a simple project and run the basic Git workflow end-to-end. Start by creating a project directory and initializing Git with git init. Create HelloWorld. java with a class that prints a greeting, then run git status to confirm the file is untracked. Stage the file with git add HelloWorld. java and commit it with a descriptive message like Initial commit: Added HelloWorld. java. Next, modify the file to add a second print statement. Run git status to see that the file is modified, then git add and git commit again with a message such as Added a second print statement. Finally run git log to observe the two commits you made. This practice reinforces the flow of edit, stage, commit, and inspect. A common beginner mistake is committing multiple unrelated changes at once; instead, make logical, small commits so the history explains the project's evolution. After finishing, ask yourself: does each commit represent one clear idea or change? If not, split the work into smaller commits next time. Hands-on: Your First Git Project Walkthrough means complete the flow of init, add, commit, modify, and log so you can repeat it confidently in future projects.. In practical terms, step-by-step terminal commands with helloworld.java. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Follow These Commands
mkdir MyJavaProject
cd MyJavaProject
git init

Example File

public class HelloWorld {

  }
}

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Beginners often make a few recurring mistakes that are easy to avoid. One mistake is forgetting to git add before committing; that results in missing changes in your commit. Another is writing vague commit messages like Changes or Fixes; these messages make the history hard to understand. A third mistake is not pulling regularly, which can produce merge conflicts and rejected pushes. To prevent these, follow best practices: run git status before staging or committing to confirm what will be recorded, craft concise commit messages that explain intent and context, and pull frequently to stay in sync with teammates. Use small, focused commits—each should represent one logical change—and prefer descriptive messages such as feat: implement user authentication rather than ambiguous verbs. Finally, use branches for features to keep the mainline stable. A helpful habit is to ask after every commit: does this message make it easy for someone else to understand why this change was made? If not, rewrite the message before pushing. These small improvements make collaboration and debugging far easier. Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Mistakes & Practices
Common Mistakes
  • Committing without staging the intended changes, leading to missing edits.
  • Vague commit messages that do not explain the reason for the change.
  • Failing to pull frequently, which increases merge conflicts and rejected pushes.
Best Practices
  • Run git status and diff tools before committing to verify content.
  • Write descriptive commit messages that explain intent and scope.
  • Commit small, logical units and pull regularly to stay in sync with the team.
Key Takeaway

Small habits—status checks, clear messages, frequent pulls—prevent most beginner Git problems.

screens.title: A Simple Team Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: A beginner-friendly team workflow uses feature branches and a central remote. Start by cloning the remote to get a local copy. Create a feature branch locally for each change to keep the main branch stable. Make small commits on your feature branch and push the branch to the remote when you're ready for review. Teammates can review and the branch is merged into main when approved. Regularly pull from main into your feature branch to incorporate others' changes and resolve conflicts early. This flow reduces risky changes on main and makes reviews easier because each pull request contains a focused set of commits. A common misconception is that all work must happen on main; instead, branches isolate work and make rollback simple. For small teams, keep the branch naming consistent, push often to back up work, and use descriptive pull request titles. After merging, delete the feature branch locally and remotely to keep the repository tidy. Ask yourself: how will you name branches and what constitutes a complete feature worth merging? A Simple Team Workflow means use feature branches, frequent small commits, pull requests for review, and regular pulls from main to collaborate safely.. fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson we move beyond writing isolated programs and learn how software engineering and version control help teams build reliable systems. Software engineering brings structure: it uses modularity to break a large problem into smaller parts, abstraction to hide unneeded details, and reusability to avoid rewriting common code. These practices make projects easier to test, maintain, and scale. Version control, and specifically Git, complements engineering by tracking every change, enabling safe experiments, and allowing teams to merge contributions without losing work. You will see how the working directory, staging area, and local repository form a simple pipeline for tracking snapshots with commands like init, add, commit, status, and log. You will also practice cloning a remote repo and sharing work with push and pull. By the end of this chapter you will be able to initialize a repository, stage and commit changes thoughtfully, read the commit history, and follow a basic collaborative workflow. This foundation is essential because confident use of Git prevents lost work and makes team development predictable. Ready to explore these practical skills and try a first Git project?

These four objectives focus your practice and show measurable progress. First, you'll explain the core principles of software engineering—modularity, abstraction, and reusability—and why those ideas guide system design and team communication. Second, you'll understand why version control systems are essential in projects, including how they prevent lost work, provide a history of changes, and enable collaboration. Third, you will initialize a local Git repository and execute the basic workflow: staging changes with add and recording snapshots with commit. Finally, you will distinguish the three Git states—working directory, staging area, and local repository—and use commands like status and log to inspect them. Each objective connects a skill to a practical benefit: better designs, safer experimentation, clear history, and smoother team sync. As you work through the chapter, use the verified competency milestones to check that you can complete each task without help, and remember that strong commit messages and frequent pulls are simple, high-impact habits.

This second objectives slide focuses on the practical actions you will take. You will learn to stage changes deliberately using git add so you choose which edits enter the next snapshot. You will write clear commit messages that explain intent and help later debugging. You will practice cloning a remote repository to get a full local copy, and you will push and pull to share and receive updates. These actions support a simple collaborative flow: clone to start, work locally with frequent commits, pull to sync others' work, and push to publish your commits. Finally, we emphasize two habits: commit meaningful units of work, and pull regularly to reduce conflicts. A quick misconception to avoid is thinking commit automatically includes all modified files—without add, changed files may remain unstaged. Each objective pairs a skill with why it matters to team productivity and project health.

Software engineering is a systematic, disciplined, and quantifiable approach to creating software that works reliably over time and across teams. At its core are principles you already know in code form: modularity breaks a large system into smaller, testable components so one change does not destabilize everything; abstraction hides implementation details so modules communicate through clear interfaces; and reusability lets you use the same component in multiple places instead of copying logic. A concrete example is designing a logging module for a Java application. Instead of sprinkling print statements throughout the code, a logging module offers a simple interface: log message and log level. Different parts of the app depend on that interface, so changing how logs are written does not require editing every class. A common misconception is that software engineering is only for large teams; in fact, these practices benefit solo projects by making them easier to navigate and extend. In practice, software engineering reduces bugs, improves onboarding for new developers, and shortens time to add new features. Reflect: when you next create a class, ask whether that class belongs to a reusable module, and how you would test it independently.

A Version Control System records changes to files over time so you can recall specific versions later. It serves three practical needs: history, collaboration, and safety. History helps you understand how and why the code evolved; collaboration lets multiple people work on the same codebase without overwriting one another; safety provides undo and branching so experiments don't break the mainline. Git is a distributed VCS, which means every developer has a full copy of the repository and its history on their machine. This local history enables fast operations and offline work. An everyday example is fixing a bug introduced two weeks ago: you use the commit history to find the change, inspect the commit message and diff, and then either revert or fix the faulty commit. A common misconception is to rely solely on file copies or zip backups; these lack structured history, metadata, and a reliable way to merge parallel work. With Git, you can branch to try a new feature, merge it once it's stable, and keep the main branch clean. Think about the last time you lost work; a VCS avoids that scenario by making snapshots explicit and reversible.

Git tracks file changes through three clear states: modified, staged, and committed. The working directory is where you edit files; changes there are local edits and not yet part of any snapshot. When you decide which edits go into the next snapshot, you stage them with git add. The staging area acts as a curated buffer so you can assemble a specific set of changes for a single logical commit. Finally, git commit writes those staged changes into the local repository as an immutable snapshot with a message describing intent. A concrete example: you add a feature and fix a typo in two separate files. By staging only the feature file, you can commit it with a focused message and stage the typo separately for its own commit. This keeps history meaningful. A common misconception is to assume git commit auto-includes all modified files; without git add, modifications remain unstaged and will not be captured. Practice the habit: edit, git status to inspect, git add the intended files, then git commit with a descriptive message. This three-step discipline leads to clear history, easier code review, and safer collaboration.

Let's walk through initializing a repository and making your first commits using a simple Java example. First, create a project directory in the terminal and run git init. This creates a hidden. git folder that stores the repository metadata. Next, create HelloWorld. java with a print statement. At this point git status will show HelloWorld. java as untracked. Use git add HelloWorld. java to stage it and then run git commit -m with a clear message describing the addition. After the commit, git status will show a clean working directory and git log will display the commit with its hash, author, date, and message. A concrete example in the terminal: mkdir MyJavaProject, cd into it, git init, create the Java file, git status, git add, git commit -m "Initial commit: Added HelloWorld. java". A common beginner mistake is committing without adding files, which either creates an empty commit or misses changes. Always run git status before committing to confirm which files are staged. End by asking: can you read the commit message you just wrote and understand the change it documents?

Understanding the difference between the working directory, staging area, and local repository is essential for predictable commits. The working directory contains the files you edit; they are your current working copy. The staging area, or index, is where you gather the specific changes you want to include in the next commit; think of it as a packing area for a snapshot. The local repository stores committed snapshots permanently on your machine's. git directory. When you run git status, Git lists files by these states, showing untracked, modified, and staged files. A practical example: if you change two files but only stage one, the commit will include only the staged file. This separation lets you craft commits that represent single logical changes—ideal for code review and debugging. A common mistake is to commit a large mixed-change snapshot with unrelated edits. To avoid this, use git add for the intended changes and commit frequently with clear messages. Reading git status and then using git diff for unstaged changes or git diff --staged for what's staged helps you verify the exact contents of a commit before creating it.

Two commands you will use constantly are git status and git log. git status reports the current state of your working directory and staging area, listing untracked, modified, and staged files. It helps you decide what to add or commit. git log shows the sequence of commits in the current branch, including each commit's hash, author, date, and message. A practical pattern is to run git status before you stage changes and to view git log after commits to confirm that the message and snapshot reflect your intent. For example, after committing an initial HelloWorld. java, git log shows your initial commit message and hash, which you can use later to reference that snapshot. A common mistake is skimming the message without confirming the diff; always use git log in combination with git show or git diff between commits to inspect the exact changes. Clear commit messages and frequent logs make it straightforward to find when a bug was introduced, who made the change, and what the rationale was. Ending question: which commit in your log best explains why a change was made?

Remote repositories hosted on services provide a central source of truth for collaboration. To get a copy of a remote repository, use git clone with the repository URL; this creates a local copy and sets the remote origin. After making local commits, use git push to upload your commits to the remote so teammates can see and integrate your work. To receive others' changes, use git pull which fetches changes and merges them into your local branch. Remember that git pull performs a fetch followed by a merge; you can also run git fetch then inspect and merge manually when you want more control. A practical pattern is: clone, create a feature branch locally, commit small units of work, pull regularly from main to stay current, resolve conflicts if needed, and push your feature branch for review. A common mistake is forgetting to pull before pushing; this can produce rejected pushes due to divergent histories and forces a merge or rebase. Practice pulling frequently and communicate with your team about branch usage. Ask yourself: how will you avoid conflicting changes if two people edit the same file in parallel?
